studyNotes.title: From Specimen to Section
studyNotes.summary: Tissue appearance depends on biology and preparation, so handling must be considered before interpreting a slide.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Fixation and preservation
Fixation stabilizes cellular components and limits autolysis. Timing, tissue thickness, and penetration affect preservation.

### Processing and embedding
Dehydration removes water, clearing agents replace alcohol, and embedding supports thin sectioning. Solvents can extract neutral lipid, so its absence from paraffin sections does not prove it was absent in vivo.

### Sectioning
A section is a two-dimensional sample of a three-dimensional structure. Oblique cuts alter profiles; serial levels may establish continuity.
keyPoints: Processing can remove substances and create apparent spaces.
mnemonics: Fix, process, embed, section: every step can change the view.

studyNotes.title: Routine Stains and Microscopy
studyNotes.summary: Common stains create contrast by interacting with tissue chemistry; no stain alone provides a complete diagnosis.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Hematoxylin and eosin
Hematoxylin commonly colors nuclei blue-purple; eosin highlights many proteins pink.

### Special stains
PAS demonstrates carbohydrate-rich structures; collagen stains distinguish connective tissue; silver methods highlight selected fibers. Controls and protocol matter.

### Microscopy workflow
Orient at low power, then inspect detail. Check focus, thickness, controls, and stain quality before concluding.
keyPoints: H&E gives broad contrast, not unique identification.
Interpret stain with morphology and quality.
mnemonics: Start broad, zoom in, and ask what the stain binds.

studyNotes.title: Artifacts and Evidence
studyNotes.summary: Artifacts can mimic tissue change; separate biological patterns from handling and sectioning effects.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Sources
Autolysis, compression, folds, chatter, stain precipitate, and extraction can alter a slide.

### Discrimination
Compare nearby regions, controls, and deeper levels. A coherent pattern that recurs is stronger evidence than one distorted profile.

### Reporting
State when orientation or preservation limits interpretation; avoid assigning biology to a feature plausibly caused by preparation.
keyPoints: Artifacts arise during collection through staining.
mnemonics: If a feature follows the workflow, check artifact before biology.

studyNotes.title: Epithelial Polarity and Junctions
studyNotes.summary: Epithelia are oriented barriers whose apical, lateral, and basal domains support distinct functions.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Domains
Apical surfaces face a lumen; lateral surfaces contact neighbors; basal surfaces attach to basement membrane. Microvilli increase area and cilia move material.

### Junctions
Tight junctions regulate paracellular passage; adherens junctions and desmosomes provide linkage; gap junctions permit communication; hemidesmosomes anchor to basal lamina.

### Renewal
Progenitors replace cells in many epithelia. Turnover and junctions maintain a controlled boundary.
keyPoints: Epithelia have apical, lateral, and basal domains.
Microvilli increase area; motile cilia move material.
mnemonics: Apical faces the lumen; basal anchors below.

studyNotes.title: Classifying Epithelia
studyNotes.summary: Classify by layer number and surface cell shape, then interpret site and function.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Layers and shapes
Simple means one layer; stratified means several. Squamous cells are flat, cuboidal roughly square, and columnar tall.

### Special patterns
Pseudostratified epithelium has nuclei at multiple levels but all cells contact basement membrane. Transitional tissue changes profile with stretch.

### Function
Thin simple epithelia favor exchange; stratified epithelia tolerate abrasion. These are tendencies, not a substitute for tissue identification.
keyPoints: Simple is one layer; stratified is multiple.
Pseudostratified appearance is not true layering.
Use anatomical site to interpret function.
mnemonics: Count layers first, then name the surface shape.

studyNotes.title: Exocrine and Endocrine Glands
studyNotes.summary: Ducts distinguish exocrine delivery from ductless endocrine release.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Exocrine
Exocrine glands deliver products to a surface by duct. Merocrine, apocrine, and holocrine describe release modes.

### Endocrine
Endocrine cells release signals into interstitial fluid near capillaries and have no duct to a surface.

### Other axes
Glands may also be simple or compound, tubular or acinar, and unicellular or multicellular. These classify different features.
keyPoints: Endocrine products enter interstitial fluid and blood.
Release modes describe how product exits.
Duct branching and release mode differ.
mnemonics: Duct route tells where; release mode tells how.

studyNotes.title: Cells and Matrix
studyNotes.summary: Connective tissue combines cells, fibers, and hydrated ground substance for support, exchange, defense, or storage.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Cells
Fibroblasts synthesize matrix. Macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells, and recruited leukocytes support defense and repair; adipocytes store lipid and signal.

### Fibers
Type I collagen provides tensile strength, type III creates reticular networks, and elastin supports recoil. Ground substance contains hydrated glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans, and adhesive glycoproteins.

### Interpretation
Consider cell abundance, fiber orientation, and matrix density together; one feature rarely establishes function.
keyPoints: Type I collagen provides tensile strength.
Type III collagen forms reticular networks.
mnemonics: Cells make the scaffold; fibers tune its mechanics.

studyNotes.title: Collagen Architecture
studyNotes.summary: Fiber arrangement matters alongside composition when inferring mechanical behavior.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Regular and irregular
Dense regular tissue aligns collagen with a dominant direction, as in tendon. Dense irregular tissue has varied orientations, as in dermis.

### Loose and reticular
Areolar tissue has more ground substance and allows exchange. Reticular tissue provides a fine framework for mobile cells.

### Caution
A section plane may distort orientation. Use multiple regions and anatomical site.
keyPoints: Parallel bundles resist force along one axis.
mnemonics: Regular runs one way; irregular spreads directions.

studyNotes.title: Adipose and Repair
studyNotes.summary: Adipose tissue is active, and matrix remodeling is central to repair.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Adipose
White adipocytes usually have one dominant droplet; brown adipocytes have multiple droplets and abundant mitochondria. Paraffin processing extracts lipid.

Inflammation, proliferation, matrix deposition, and remodeling overlap. Fibroblasts produce collagen while vessels and immune cells shape repair.

A single field may not represent the full repair stage. Interpret distribution and context.
keyPoints: White adipocytes usually have one large droplet.
Brown adipocytes have multiple droplets and mitochondria.
Repair includes matrix deposition and remodeling.
mnemonics: Repair lays matrix, then remodels its arrangement.

studyNotes.title: Cartilage Types
studyNotes.summary: Cartilage matrix and fiber organization determine mechanical behavior.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Hyaline
Type II collagen and proteoglycans create a hydrated matrix for compression at joints, airways, and growth plates.

### Elastic and fibrocartilage
Elastic fibers allow recoil in the external ear. Fibrocartilage has abundant type I collagen and tolerates combined tensile and compressive stress.

### Growth and nutrition
Cartilage is avascular; nutrients diffuse from surrounding fluid or perichondrium where present. Interstitial growth occurs internally; appositional growth adds at a surface.
keyPoints: Hyaline has type II collagen and proteoglycans.
Fibrocartilage has abundant type I collagen.
mnemonics: Hyaline hydrates; elastic recoils; fibrocartilage reinforces.

studyNotes.title: Bone Cells and Remodeling
studyNotes.summary: Bone is dynamic mineralized tissue maintained by formation, resorption, and sensing.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Cell roles
Osteoblasts make osteoid and support mineralization. Osteocytes sense mechanical conditions. Osteoclasts resorb matrix and derive from hematopoietic precursors.

### Remodeling
Resorption is followed by formation; coupling renews or adapts matrix. Imbalance changes mass and architecture.

### Composite matrix
Type I collagen provides tensile framework; hydroxyapatite adds stiffness and compressive strength.
keyPoints: Osteoblasts form; osteocytes sense; osteoclasts resorb.
Collagen and mineral provide different properties.
mnemonics: Blasts build, cytes sense, clasts clear.

studyNotes.title: Bone Growth and Interfaces
studyNotes.summary: Bone develops through distinct modes, with interfaces that distribute force.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Formation modes
Intramembranous ossification forms bone directly from mesenchyme. Endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model. Growth plates organize chondrocyte maturation and replacement.

### Entheses
Attachment zones may transition through fibrocartilage toward mineralized tissue, helping manage stiffness differences.

### Reading sections
Identify matrix, cell, and spatial sequence together; a section can capture one stage only.
keyPoints: Intramembranous bone forms directly from mesenchyme.
mnemonics: Endochondral means cartilage first, bone follows.

studyNotes.title: Peripheral Blood Morphology
studyNotes.summary: Blood cells are distinguished by size, nuclear features, granules, and cytoplasmic staining.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Erythrocytes and platelets
Mature erythrocytes are anucleate and hemoglobin-rich. Platelets are small fragments from megakaryocytes.

### Leukocytes
Neutrophils have segmented nuclei; eosinophils have prominent eosinophilic granules; basophils have dark granules. Monocytes have folded nuclei; lymphocytes commonly have dense nuclei with scant cytoplasm.

### Smear interpretation
Preparation and timing affect morphology. Correlate suspected changes with counts and confirmatory evidence.
keyPoints: Red cells are anucleate and contain hemoglobin.
Leukocyte ID uses nucleus and granules.
mnemonics: Name nucleus, granules, and cytoplasm before naming the cell.

studyNotes.title: Hematopoiesis and Marrow
studyNotes.summary: Marrow maintains blood production through progenitors supported by a stromal niche.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Lineages
Stem cells produce progenitors that mature into erythroid, myeloid, and lymphoid cells. Maturation changes nuclear condensation, cytoplasm, and granules.

### Specialized pathways
Erythroid cells condense and expel the nucleus. Megakaryocytes undergo endomitosis and extend platelet-forming processes.

### Niche
Stroma, matrix, vessels, and signals regulate maturation. Aspirate and biopsy sample different features.
mnemonics: Marrow makes lineages; the niche guides maturation.

studyNotes.title: Lymphoid Organs
studyNotes.summary: Lymph nodes filter lymph, whereas spleen surveys blood; compartment organization reflects antigen route.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Node
Cortex contains B-cell follicles and possible germinal centers. Paracortex is T-cell rich and has high endothelial venules. Medullary cords and sinuses support passage and filtration.

### Spleen
White pulp surrounds arteries; red pulp cords and sinusoids filter blood and remove aged erythrocytes.

### Comparison
Use vascular relationships and compartments to distinguish organs.
keyPoints: Nodes filter lymph; spleen filters blood.
Splenic red pulp removes aged red cells.
mnemonics: Node: lymph routes; spleen: blood routes.

studyNotes.title: Skeletal Muscle Organization
studyNotes.summary: Skeletal muscle is organized from whole organ to fascicles, fibers, myofibrils, and sarcomeres.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Coverings
Endomysium surrounds each fiber, perimysium each fascicle, and epimysium the whole muscle. These layers carry vessels and transmit force.

### Sarcomere
Actin and myosin form repeating units between Z discs. Alignment creates striations; contraction slides filaments rather than shortening them.

### Repair
Satellite cells lie between sarcolemma and basal lamina. They support regeneration, but severe injury may lead to fibrosis.
keyPoints: Fibers are multinucleated with peripheral nuclei.
mnemonics: Muscle coverings carry force from fiber to organ.

studyNotes.title: Cardiac Muscle
studyNotes.summary: Cardiac muscle combines striated contractile machinery with junctions that coordinate pumping.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Cells and discs
Cardiomyocytes branch and usually have one central nucleus. Intercalated discs contain fascia adherens and desmosomes for mechanical strength, plus gap junctions for electrical coupling.

### Integration
Activation spreads through connected myocardium. Coordinated behavior depends on excitability and intact cell junctions.

### Distinction
Striations reflect sarcomeres, while branching and intercalated discs distinguish cardiac from skeletal muscle.
keyPoints: Cardiomyocytes branch and have central nuclei.
Discs combine mechanical and electrical junctions.
Cardiac muscle is striated but distinct.
mnemonics: Discs hold cardiac cells together and let activation pass.

studyNotes.title: Smooth Muscle
studyNotes.summary: Smooth muscle regulates hollow-organ movement and lumen size without visible sarcomeric stripes.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Structure
Cells are spindle-shaped with a central nucleus. Actin and myosin attach to dense bodies rather than repeating Z discs.

### Contraction
Calcium-dependent pathways regulate contraction without the troponin arrangement of striated muscle. Force may be graded and sustained.

### Organization
Circumferential vascular muscle changes caliber; coordinated organ layers move contents.
keyPoints: Smooth cells are spindle-shaped and nonstriated.
Contraction is involuntary and can be sustained.
mnemonics: Smooth muscle adjusts tubes; it has no visible sarcomere stripes.

studyNotes.title: Neurons and Synapses
studyNotes.summary: Neurons are polarized signaling cells connected into circuits through synapses.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Neuronal regions
The soma contains the nucleus and biosynthetic machinery. Dendrites and soma commonly receive input; the axon conducts toward terminals.

### Synapses
Chemical synapses release transmitter across a cleft; electrical synapses use gap junctions. Location and structure influence signal integration.

### Context
Neuron shape varies by location. Identify processes and neighboring glia in context rather than infer a circuit from one cell.
keyPoints: Dendrites commonly receive; axons send output.
mnemonics: Dendrites receive; the axon sends toward a target.

studyNotes.title: Glial Cells
studyNotes.summary: Glia maintain the neural environment, support signaling, insulate axons, and participate in immune surveillance.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### CNS
Astrocytes regulate ions and transmitters; oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; microglia provide immune surveillance; ependymal cells line ventricles.

### PNS
Schwann cells support axons and form myelin. Satellite glia surround neuronal cell bodies in ganglia.

### Identification
Use location, morphology, and markers because processes may be inconspicuous in routine stains.
mnemonics: Oligodendrocytes in CNS; Schwann cells in PNS.

studyNotes.title: Myelin and Axonal Conduction
studyNotes.summary: Myelin changes axonal electrical properties and organizes propagation between nodes.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Internodes and nodes
Myelin wraps internodes; nodes of Ranvier are gaps enriched in channels where action potentials regenerate.

### Cell sources
One oligodendrocyte may myelinate segments on several CNS axons. A Schwann cell typically myelinates one PNS internode.

### Interpretation
Myelin disruption can alter timing and conduction, but histology alone does not establish cause.
mnemonics: Nodes renew the signal between insulated segments.

studyNotes.title: Skin Layers and Renewal
studyNotes.summary: The integument combines renewing epithelium, connective dermis, vascular supply, and appendages.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Epidermis
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium renews from basal keratinocytes that differentiate toward the surface. Melanocytes, immune cells, and Merkel cells add specialized roles.

### Dermis
Papillary dermis is superficial and looser; reticular dermis is denser and collagen-rich. Vessels, nerves, follicles, and glands reside here.

### Skin types
Thick skin has a thick stratum corneum and lacks follicles and sebaceous glands. Thin skin contains follicles and associated glands.
keyPoints: Epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous tissue.
mnemonics: Epidermis renews upward; dermis supplies below.

studyNotes.title: Vessel Walls and Endothelium
studyNotes.summary: Vessel architecture reflects pressure, flow, and exchange requirements.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Tunics
Intima includes endothelium; media contains smooth muscle and elastic components; adventitia anchors the vessel. Proportions vary.

### Arteries and veins
Muscular arteries regulate distribution. Veins generally have thinner walls relative to lumen and may contain valves. Elastic arteries have prominent lamellae.

### Microvessels
Capillaries have endothelium and basal lamina, sometimes with pericytes. Thin walls support exchange; permeability varies by capillary type.
mnemonics: Intima lines, media moves, adventitia anchors.

studyNotes.title: Cutaneous Glands and Exchange
studyNotes.summary: Skin appendages and dermal microvessels support secretion, thermoregulation, and barrier maintenance.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Sweat glands
Eccrine glands deliver sweat to the surface. Apocrine glands open into follicles in selected regions.

### Sebaceous glands
Sebaceous glands commonly empty into follicles and release sebum holocrinely. Their association with follicles explains absence in glabrous thick skin.

### Microcirculation
Dermal blood flow contributes to nutrient supply and heat exchange. Epidermis is avascular and receives nutrients by diffusion.
keyPoints: Epidermis depends on diffusion from dermis.
Dermal blood flow contributes to heat exchange.
mnemonics: Eccrine exits to surface; sebaceous joins the follicle.
